tasks.short: Chart interventions, write the shift evaluation per care problem, revise the plan and prepare the handover summary.

steps.what: Nurse charts interventions at the bedside during the shift
Nurse writes the shift evaluation of outcomes for each care problem

loop.input: The nurse's dictated one-minute summary per care problem plus the shift's charted interventions, vitals, fluid balance and scores.
loop.output: A draft evaluation per care problem: what was done, the outcome against the goal, and open issues.
loop.check: Every number and time must match a charted entry; each care problem in the plan gets a section or is marked 'not evaluated'; statements not in the dictation or the chart are removed; the nurse validates before saving.
loop.stop: One draft per shift; on failure the nurse writes the evaluation.
loop.why_not_simpler: The nurse's reasoning about outcomes is spoken free text; a template only lists the charted values.

steps.what: Nurse revises treatment plans: problems, goals and interventions in free text
Nurse writes the handover summary for the next shift
Intensivist reads the nursing documentation on rounds
Nurse completes entries flagged as missing by the documentation audit

tasks.design: At the end of the shift the nurse dictates a short summary per care problem; a bounded step drafts the evaluation from it and the charted data in the patient data system ({OTHER}), and the nurse validates it before saving. Care plan revisions use the unit's standard problem and intervention library, the handover summary is generated from the evaluation and plan, and a completeness check runs before the nurse signs off instead of in a later audit.
tasks.previous_blocker: Evaluations were typed from memory at the end of a busy shift, and gaps surfaced weeks later in audits.
tasks.enabler_now: Dutch scribes produce notes clinicians validate, and records support care plan libraries and completeness checks.
tasks.still_hard: Drafts can state outcomes the nurse did not mean; the inspectorate expects testing, training and monitoring of generative tools.
tasks.human_edge: Judging whether the patient is truly getting better and writing what the next nurse must watch.
tasks.altitude: The nurse validates drafts instead of typing evaluations; plan decisions stay theirs.

reach.task: Write daily evaluations in the care plan
reach.learn: Whether dictated drafts work with fewer charted values.

evidence.claim: A Dutch scribe records, the clinician validates, and the note goes into the hospital record.
Self-estimated time per note fell 29% across 236,153 scribe notes, with median editing of 93 seconds; three of seven authors were from the vendor.
Providers are responsible for careful use of generative AI: assess risks, train, test and monitor after updates.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from charting during the shift to the handover summary; the handover talk is outside.

Input contract: charted interventions, vitals and balances entered or validated by nurses; care plan problem and intervention library kept by the unit's nursing documentation group; today's documentation audit list produced by the quality nurse, replaced by the end-of-shift completeness check; fallback is typing.
Drafting runs in the hospital's governed environment under a processing agreement.
Intensivist time is outside the nurse's savings.
unknowns: How long evaluations take per shift today.
Whether the unit has a care plan library.
research_questions: How often do nurses change outcome statements in the drafts?

already_counted.description: Nurse validates the drafted evaluation per care problem.
Nurse checks the generated handover summary.

incremental.description: Nurse dictates summaries and reports draft errors.
Clinical informatics audits draft samples and monitors after updates.

approvals.approved_version: Evaluation text as validated by the nurse before saving; later edits are a new version.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Nurses who rewrite most drafts, or shifts with a crisis that leaves no time to dictate, save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Screen nutritional status on admission, track feeding against targets, judge complication risk and involve the dietitian.

steps.what: Nurse asks the patient or family about weight loss and intake before admission
Nurse weighs the patient or estimates weight and height
Nurse calculates the nutritional screening score on a paper form
Nurse adds up delivered feeding and checks it against the target by hand
Nurse judges the risk of complications such as refeeding, pressure ulcers and weakness
Nurse phones the dietitian to request an assessment
Dietitian assesses the patient and sets the feeding plan

tasks.design: The screening form in the patient data system ({OTHER}) computes the score from the nurse's answers and the recorded weight and height, and a score above the hospital's threshold creates a dietitian referral automatically; the nurse can still refer others. A feeding view computes each patient's energy and protein target from weight and compares it with delivered feeding volumes, flagging days under target.
tasks.previous_blocker: Screening was a paper form and delivered calories were added up by hand, if at all.
tasks.enabler_now: Records support scored forms, rule-based referrals and computed targets as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Weight in critical illness is often estimated, and risk depends on the whole clinical picture.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting the patient who is wasting despite a normal score and pushing for the dietitian early.

ambition.what: Feeding checked against target every day for every patient, not only those already under the dietitian.

tasks.altitude: The nurse confirms scores and reads one view; feeding decisions stay with the dietitian and intensivist.

reach.learn: Whether automatic referrals overload or focus their list.

evidence.claim: Records can compute screening scores, create referrals by rule and show intake against computed targets.
Solely automated decisions with significant effect need a legal basis; an internal referral from a confirmed score leaves the decision with clinicians.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from admission screening to the dietitian's feeding plan; feeding itself is outside.

Input contract: weight and height entered by the nurse; feeding volumes from feeding pumps or entered hourly by nurses in the patient data system; target formula and referral threshold set by the dietitians; fallback is the paper form and a phone call.
Dietitian time is outside the nurse's savings.
Interview, weighing and the risk judgement do not change.
unknowns: Whether feeding volumes are recorded hourly today.
Share of patients referred to the dietitian.
research_questions: Do daily intake-against-target flags shorten time under target?

already_counted.description: Nurse confirms the computed screening score.
Nurse reviews days flagged under target.

incremental.description: Nurse records weight and feeding volumes consistently.
Dietitians keep target formulas and the referral threshold current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units where feeding volumes are not charted hourly cannot compute delivered intake and keep hand counts.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Talk with patient and family about sleep, fear, grief and anger, observe, record the findings and arrange support.

steps.what: Nurse talks with patients and family about worries, grief, anger and support systems
Nurse observes sleep patterns, anxiety and agitation during the shift
Nurse writes the psychosocial findings as free text in the record
Nurse phones the social worker, spiritual counsellor or psychologist to ask for support
Social worker or spiritual counsellor visits the patient and family
Nurse adjusts care: quiet hours, visiting arrangements and sleep measures

tasks.design: Configure a short structured psychosocial form in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) with the unit's sleep and anxiety scales and a family support section, so findings are comparable across shifts. Support requests become referral orders with a reason to social work, spiritual care or psychology instead of phone calls; the conversations stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Findings were scattered in free-text notes and requests depended on reaching someone by phone.
tasks.enabler_now: Records support structured forms and referral orders as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Psychosocial assessment is a relationship; forms risk turning it into ticking boxes.
tasks.human_edge: Staying with a frightened patient or a grieving family and noticing what they cannot say.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; findings are easier to follow across shifts.

reach.task: Receive and prioritise support requests from the ICU
reach.learn: Whether written reasons help them prioritise visits.

evidence.claim: Records support structured assessment forms and referral orders to other disciplines.
Health data is special category data under the GDPR.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from the conversation to adjusted care and support arranged; therapy by others is outside.
Input contract: scales chosen by the unit's nursing quality group; referral reasons list agreed with social work and spiritual care; fallback is phone and free text.
Social worker time is outside the nurse's savings.
Conversations, observation and care adjustments do not change.
unknowns: Which scales the unit uses today.
How often support is requested per week.
research_questions: Do structured findings lead to earlier referrals for families in distress?

incremental.description: Nurse learns the form and its scales.
Social work keeps the referral reasons list current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Nurses who keep writing free text alongside the form, or units with few referrals, save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Screen older patients for frailty, find age-specific needs with patient and family, and adjust the care plan.

steps.what: Nurse reviews age, history and home situation in the record
Nurse completes the frailty screening for older patients: delirium, falls, function
Nurse identifies age-specific needs with patient and family: hearing, sight, routines, schooling
Nurse alters care plans by typing delirium, fall and family measures
Geriatric consult team advises on frail older patients
Nurse explains the changed approach to colleagues at handover

tasks.design: The frailty screening opens automatically in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) for patients aged 70 and over and pre-fills items already captured at admission, such as living situation and walking aid. Screening results map by fixed rules to standard interventions in the unit's care plan library (delirium prevention, fall measures, family involvement), which the nurse accepts or changes.
tasks.previous_blocker: Screenings repeated questions already asked at admission, and plan measures were typed from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Records support age-triggered forms, pre-fill and rule-based care plan suggestions as configuration.
tasks.still_hard: Needs differ by person, not only by age; fixed suggestions can become automatic plans nobody reads.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing what an old man or a teenager needs to stay oriented and calm in an ICU.

ambition.what: Every older patient screened on the first day, with prevention measures in the plan from the start.

tasks.altitude: The nurse accepts or changes suggestions; plan decisions stay theirs.

reach.task: Select ICU patients for a geriatric consult
reach.learn: Whether screening results help them choose whom to see.

evidence.claim: Records support age-triggered screening forms and rule-based care plan suggestions.
Providers are responsible for careful introduction and testing of new software in care.
The record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from reviewing the patient's background to the team informed; care itself is outside.

Input contract: admission data (living situation, walking aid, home care) entered by the admitting nurse; screening items and intervention rules set by the hospital's geriatric team; fallback is the paper screening.
Geriatrician time is outside the nurse's savings.
The conversation and handover do not change.
unknowns: Share of ICU patients aged 70 and over.
Whether the unit has a care plan library.
research_questions: Do first-day screenings lower delirium days?

already_counted.description: Nurse reviews the suggested interventions before accepting them.

incremental.description: Nurse completes missing admission items the screening needs.
Geriatric team keeps screening items and rules current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Units with mostly younger trauma patients rarely trigger the screening and save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The critical care nurse keeps conversations, judgement and care decisions; evaluations, screenings and referrals become drafts and forms to check.
skills_to_grow: Dictating clear evaluations and validating drafts
Using screening results without losing the person
role.ambitious_version: A critical care nurse whose documentation is checked rather than typed, with nutrition, frailty and family needs picked up on day one.
